entries.title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinian homes in West Bank
entries.summary: Masked Israeli settlers launched their first major attack since initiating a siege in the village of Qusra earlier this month. Saturday's attacks were met with rare criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
entries.content:
Middle East

Israeli settlers attack Palestinian homes in West Bank

August 29, 2026

Masked Israeli settlers launched their first major attack since initiating a siege in the village of Qusra earlier this month. Saturday's attacks were met with rare criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, pelting them with rocks and trapping residents in their homes.

The incident was the first major attack by Israeli settlers since they began a siege in the villages of Qusra and neighboring Jalud earlier this month.

On Saturday, settlers descended on Qusra and began pelting Palestinians with rocks. When dozens of residents sought to barricade themselves in a home, settlers followed them in, according to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).

"The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside the house," said an IDF statement.

Who is the IDF protecting in such situations?

Although the IDF said settler vehicles had been impounded and authorities were gathering evidence, Palestinian media said the IDF protected the settlers during the melee.

A number of Palestinians said they were injured after being pepper sprayed by settlers, and reported that other Israeli settlers had tried to burn nearby fields owned by Palestinians.

One Palestinian said the IDF had fired tear gas into the home that he was in and held several people inside while at the same time letting Israeli settlers go free.

Other Palestinians said IDF officers had handcuffed, blindfolded and beaten residents trapped inside before letting them go.

Local Palestinians told international news teams that they had been trapped in their homes for hours waiting for help from the IDF.

The IDF did not comment on the use of tear gas nor accusations of handcuffs and beatings.

Saturday attacks elicit rare criticism from Netanyahu

Saturday's attacks took place just yards away from three other Qusra homes that radical Jewish settlers targeted in a siege that began three weeks ago.

Despite a massive Israeli military presence that local Palestinians say has kept them imprisoned in their houses, residents report near-daily settler encroachments.

Rights groups say settler aggression is part of an — illegal — effort to seize land from residents in the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians hope to one day found their own independent state. The Israeli government has rejected accusations of illegality. Various Israeli political figures have justified the settlements for security reasons or argued there are biblical grounds for the creation of the settlements.

The IDF has said it will continue "to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area."

Although settlers have been emboldened by the stance of Israel's far-right government — which has encouraged settlement building despite broad international opposition — the Saturday attack managed to elicit rare criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

On Saturday, Netanyahu released a statement on X saying, "I strongly condemn the criminal acts of violence committed in the villages of Qusra and Jalud by a handful of rioters who are violating the law, causing a grave injustice to the law-abiding Jewish community, interfering with the IDF in carrying out its missions, and harming Israel's standing in the world."

Increasing Israeli settler violence has even garnered criticism from US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who recently denounced radical settlers in the West Bank as "Israeli terrorists," adding that those behind the siege of Qusra could face US sanctions.

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Zimbabwe crash involving church minibus kills 27
entries.summary: Dozens of people were killed when a minibus carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck in central Zimbabwe. The crash near the town of Chivhu is the latest deadly road accident in the African country.
entries.content:
Africa

Zimbabwe crash involving church minibus kills 27

August 29, 2026

Dozens of people were killed when a minibus carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck in central Zimbabwe. The crash near the town of Chivhu is the latest deadly road accident in the African country.

At least 27 people were killed in a minibus crash in central Zimbabwe after the vehicle carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck, police said Saturday. Seven people were injured.

Police spokesperson Paul Nyathi said members of a popular Indigenous African Christian denomination, known for wearing white robes, were traveling to a conference on Friday when their minibus collided with a truck on a major highway near the town of Chivhu, about 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of the capital, Harare.

The foreign-registered haulage truck was overtaking another vehicle when it collided with the minibus. Both vehicles were carrying an "unspecified" number of passengers, Nyathi said in a statement.

Footage shared on social media by public broadcaster ZBC showed the mangled minibus charred to a shell.

Zimbabwe faces road safety crisis

Authorities say 94% of road accidents occur due to human error. Many Zimbabweans rely on privately operated minibus taxis, known locally as kombis, for everyday transportation. The vehicles are often criticized for carrying more passengers than allowed.

Zimbabwe’s roads are also riddled with potholes after years of underfunding and neglect, while driving standards can be poor.

In April, at least 18 people were killed when a minibus burst into flames on a highway in southern Zimbabwe. Earlier that month, a woman and her five children were killed when their vehicle collided with a haulage truck on another highway linking Zimbabwe and South Africa.



Road crashes kill about 300,000 people across Africa each year, accounting for roughly a quarter of the global road death toll, according to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. The continent has the world’s highest road fatality rate, the commission says.

This is despite Africa’s 1.5 billion people accounting for only about 3% of the world’s vehicle fleet.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Russian-American heads Trump's planned Caucasus trade route
entries.summary: A Russian-born businessman heads the investment fund financing the so-called "Trump Route," a planned corridor through Armenia linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. Who is Konstantin Sokolov, and what role does he play?
entries.content:
August 29, 2026

A Russian-born businessman heads the investment fund financing the so-called "Trump Route," a planned corridor through Armenia linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. Who is Konstantin Sokolov, and what role does he play?

Until recently, few people in the South Caucasus had heard of Konstantin Sokolov. Now the 52-year-old Russian-American businessman is at the center of new investment fund backed by US President Donald Trump. 

In mid-July, Sokolov — who emigrated from Russia to the US at age 21 and later founded the investment firm IJS Investments in Chicago — was appointed to head a new investment fund of the US State Department.

The TRIPP+ EnterpriseFund, registered in the US as the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund and launched with more than $200 million (about €172.5 million) in capital, is expected to invest in countries across the South Caucasus and Central Asia and help finance the large-scale TRIPP infrastructure project, also known as the "Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity."

The "Trump Route" is a transit corridor that aims to connect Azerbaijan with its autonomous exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. The ambitious infrastructure project is part of a peace deal that Armenia and Azerbaijan signed in August 2025 with US mediation. In early June 2026, Washington and Yerevan signed a framework cooperation agreement for the project.

Experts have said construction of the "Trump Route" fits Washington's strategy of creating a trade corridor between Europe and the region that bypasses existing routes through Russia and Iran.

Sokolov buys up Russian assets in Armenia

Long before he was appointed to head TRIPP+, Sokolov had already established a foothold in Armenia.

In 2024, he acquired Viva Armenia, the country's largest telecommunications provider. Despite its subsequent partial nationalization, Sokolov continued to expand his holdings. Recently, his companies also bought up the Armenian subsidiary of Russian telecom giant Rostelecom.

An even more significant deal, however, was carried out largely out of the public eye: the purchase of the Teghut copper-molybdenum mine. The mine, which holds an estimated 450 million metric tons of ore and has Armenia's second-largest reserves, had been taken over by Russia's state-owned VTB Bank after the company accumulated massive debts. VTB is now under Western sanctions. According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty's Armenian service, the deal was carried out through a third-party company.

"Sokolov wanted to avoid a direct deal with the Russian bank," said Mkrtich Karapetyan, a Radio Liberty journalist who has been investigating the flow of foreign capital into Armenia.

Sokolov: Trump supporter, MAGA backer

While Armenia's government and its supporters have welcomed the influx of Western capital into the country's infrastructure projects, the opposition has highlighted serious risks.

Mesrop Manukyan, a lawmaker from the opposition Armenia Alliance, is among Sokolov's most vocal critics in parliament. He said it's alarming that a US investor has been able to acquire major stakes in the finance, mining and telecommunications sectors in just a few years.

Manukyan's faction, which advocates close ties between Armenia and Russia, opposes the TRIPP+ project. It views the "Trump Route" as a disguised "extraterritorial corridor" and the "greatest threat" to Armenia's security.

Despite his extensive investments, Sokolov remains largely unknown to the Armenian public. There are no official photos of him, and he generally avoids interviews with the local press during business trips.

His most recent visit to the capital, Yerevan, was in early August, when he met with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan. He was accompanied by Aryeh Lightstone, senior adviser to US special envoy Steve Witkoff.

In Western media, however, Sokolov is known not only for his business ventures in the US and Switzerland but also for his political involvement. Sokolov is a major donor to the US Republican Party and a Trump supporter. According to The Associated Press, he donated about $11 million to Trump's MAGA movement over the course of a year.

'Compromise' between Moscow and Washington?

Benyamin Poghosyan of the Armenian think tank APRI sees two main reasons for Sokolov's appointment to head the fund.

The first is political. Appointing an American with Russian roots could be "a subtle gesture by Washington aimed at easing Moscow's fierce criticism of the project," he told DW.

The second, however, is pragmatic. "Perhaps Russia has nothing to do with it at all. Sokolov may simply have been chosen because he has a deep understanding of the business environment in the former Soviet Union — and because he knows Armenia and how its government works," said Poghosyan.

At the same time, the sheer scale of the investment and the financier's Russian roots are fueling speculation in Armenia. Social media users in the country are debating whether Sokolov, who was born in St. Petersburg, could be a secret "compromise figure" between Moscow and Washington. Supporters of the theory point to the ease with which US companies have acquired formerly Russian assets subject to Western sanctions.

Other observers have refuted the idea, noting that Sokolov has publicly and sharply criticized the Russian government and its war against Ukraine. The funds provided by the US State Department, running through 2036, are seen as flagging Washington's long-term strategic intentions in the region. During his visit to Yerevan, Aryeh Lightstone told Armenian news outlet CivilNet that the more than $200 million in initial funding could be viewed as a starting point for future investments.

Aram Sargsyan, head of the Republican Party of Armenia and an ally of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, also rejects the idea that Sokolov is a "compromise figure" for Moscow. He emphasized the practical value of Sokolov's background, seeing it as an opportunity rather than a cause for concern.

"Sokolov has significant business contacts, understands the Russian mentality perfectly, speaks the language and knows how to work with relevant Russian institutions," he said.

This article was originally written in Russian.

entries.title: Saxony-Anhalt election: Why the AfD is so strong
entries.summary: The AfD is polling above 40% ahead of Saxony-Anhalt's election on September 6. What is driving support for the far right in this predominantly rural eastern German state?
entries.content:
Germany

Saxony-Anhalt election: Why the AfD is so strong

August 29, 2026

The AfD is polling above 40% ahead of Saxony-Anhalt's election on September 6. What is driving support for the far right in this predominantly rural eastern German state?

Saxony-Anhalt, one of Germany's 16 federal states, boasts a rich cultural and historical heritage. 

Many of the world-famous architects associated with the Bauhaus in Dessau lived and worked here. The towns of Eisleben and, above all, Wittenberg preserve the memory of the great reformer Martin Luther. It was in Wittenberg that he famously nailed his 95 theses to the door of the Castle Church, setting the Reformation in motion.

Saxony-Anhalt is also home to the Chemical Triangle around Leuna and Bitterfeld in the eastern part of the state, which still accounts for around 10,000 jobs. To the west lies the Harz mountain range, while the Elbe River, one of Europe's major waterways, flows through the state from southeast to north.

The southern part of Saxony-Anhalt is being forced to reinvent itself as it undergoes structural change following the decision to phase out lignite coal. Unemployment remains slightly above the national average.

Home to around 2.1 million people, it is one of Germany's more sparsely populated states. Only two cities, the state capital Magdeburg and Halle, have more than 200,000 inhabitants.

Nevertheless, in September, international attention is likely to turn to this small eastern German state. For the first time in postwar German history, a candidate from a party that Germany's domestic intelligence agency has classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" in parts could become the head of a state government. The Alternative for Germany (AfD), whose lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, holds a clear lead in all opinion polls.

AfD far ahead in latest polls

Just before the election, the AfD is polling at more than 40% in Saxony-Anhalt. The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which has been the dominant governing party in the state since German reunification in 1990, trails far behind, with support ranging between 23% and 26%.

The state office for the protection of the constitution has classified the AfD as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization, but this has done little to dent its popularity among voters. The Left Party is polling at 13%, while support for the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) stands at between 6% and 7%. It remains uncertain whether the Greens and the pro-business Free Democratic Party (FDP) will succeed in returning to the state parliament.

CDU politician Reiner Haseloff served as state premier of Saxony-Anhalt for 15 years before stepping down in January 2026. In an interview with Der Spiegel, Haseloff said he had often felt, while sitting in the state parliament in Magdeburg, "as though I were in the final phase of the Weimar Republic's Reichstag, or later in Berlin's Sportpalast."

The Weimar Republic, Germany's first democracy, came to an end in 1933 when the Nazis seized power. It was in Berlin's Sportpalast that Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, a close confidant of Adolf Hitler, delivered his notorious 1943 "total war" speech.

Haseloff's successor, Sven Schulze, also of the CDU, must now take on the AfD in the upcoming election. If he fails, the CDU's long dominance of state politics could come to an end. Most recently, the conservatives governed in coalition with the Social Democrats and the FDP.

Saxony-Anhalt's unusual political history

From 1994 to 2002, Saxony-Anhalt was also at the center of national political attention. In July 1994, the Social Democrat Reinhard Höppner formed a minority government with the ecologist Greens that relied on the support of the left-wing Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), successor to East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party.

Just five years after the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, cooperation with the heirs to East Germany's former ruling party was widely seen across the country, especially by conservatives, as crossing a political red line.

Support for extremist parties has long been stronger in Saxony-Anhalt than in many other parts of Germany. In 1998, the far-right German People's Union (DVU), classified as right-wing extremist, won 12.9% of the vote and entered the state parliament. However, internal divisions within the party were so deep that it chose not to contest the 2002 state election.

What's driving AfD support in Saxony-Anhalt?

Experts attribute the AfD's strong showing in the polls largely to the widespread dissatisfaction many people in the state feel with developments in Germany. Many jobs disappeared in the years following reunification, particularly in the lignite mining and chemical industries.

Saxony-Anhalt also faces pronounced demographic challenges. With an average age of 48.3 years, it had Germany's oldest population in 2024. The state also has a pronounced gender imbalance among younger age groups, with approximately 120,240 men aged 18 to 29 compared with around 103,177 women. At the end of 2025, foreign nationals accounted for about 9% of the population, compared with roughly 15% nationwide. Many young people left the state and never returned.

Many people oppose further immigration, even though the state's foreign population remains comparatively small. Nevertheless, its size has increased markedly over the past decade. According to the state's Statistical Office, the number of people without German citizenship has more than doubled since 2015.

What would AfD rule mean for Saxony-Anhalt?

According to many observers, the success of the far-right DVU some 25 years ago demonstrates that right-wing extremist parties have long had a loyal core electorate in Saxony-Anhalt. Today, that electorate largely backs the AfD, regardless of its election manifesto or policy program.

Political scientist Benjamin Höhne of the Chemnitz University of Technology told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that he believes the AfD would seek to reshape the constitutional order if it were to take power in Saxony-Anhalt. Liberal democratic and rule-of-law principles, he argued, would be systematically eroded.

"I think the AfD is currently watching the United States very closely," he said. In his view, President Donald Trump's administration in the US is pursuing a similar course.

Höhne believes, however, that such radical agendas would be difficult to implement in a single federal state. "You cannot simply pull a lever in one state and expect everything to fall into line with a far-right script," he said.

One thing seems certain: on September 6, all eyes will be on this small state in the center of Germany.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: India news: PM Modi in Uzbekistan on way to SCO summit
entries.summary: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is in Uzbekistan for a two-day state visit, after which he will go to Kyrgyzstan for the SCO Summit. Meanwhile, hundreds of Indians are still missing in Nepal. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: PM Modi in Uzbekistan on way to SCO summit

Published August 29, 2026last updated August 29, 2026

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is in Uzbekistan for a two-day state visit, after which he will go to Kyrgyzstan for the SCO Summit. Meanwhile, hundreds of Indians are still missing in Nepal. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has arrived in Uzbekistan for bilateral talks
  • Hundreds of Indians remain missing in Nepal floods
  • Indian opposition claims Sonia Gandhi's memoir dropped by Penguin India over Modi, RSS and China
  • Controversial Hindu nationalist group chief Mohan Bhagwat set to deliver speech in NYC

Here are the biggest headlines from India on Saturday, August 29, and Sunday, August 30.

We're pausing our coverage

We're pausing our India news coverage for Saturday.

Skip next section Modi lands in Uzbekistan en route to Russia-Asia summit

Modi lands in Uzbekistan en route to Russia-Asia summit

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi posted pictures of himself and Uzbekistan's President Shavkat Mirziyoyev to social media on Saturday, thanking his political counterpart for the warm welcome and writing on X: "Landed in Tashkent to a warm welcome by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. Grateful to him for the special gesture." 

Modi went on to emphasize, "This is my fourth visit to Uzbekistan, reflecting the depth and growing momentum of our bilateral relations."

Modi is scheduled to attend dinner with Mirziyoyev on Saturday.

The two will hold bilateral meetings on Sunday before departing for the Kyrgyz Republic and the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit. 

Modi is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Kyrgyz summit.

Skip next section Kolkata Police file First Information Report against former West Bengal Chief Minister Banerjee

Kolkata Police file First Information Report against former West Bengal Chief Minister Banerjee

Kolkata Police on Saturday registered a First Information Report (FIR) against former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee for allegedly violating a Calcutta High Court order on a students' wing rally held on Friday.

A FIR is written document informing police of a crime and gives the authorities necessary information to launch an investigation.

Several Indian media outlets reported on the FIR. A Hindustan Times report said that the city's high court had permitted Banerjee to celebrate the foundation day of her party's youth wing on Cathedral Road in central Kolkata but had directed that one side of the road be kept operational.

Local police said that the flank was not left open and the court-specified time-limit was exceeded.

The FIR was filed against Banerjee and organizers of the rally, officers quoted by news agency Press Trust of India said.

"The FIR has been registered for the alleged violation of the court's order. The role of all those involved in the violation will be examined during the course of the investigation," the officer said.

The police also claimed the student wing supporters "breached barricades and jostled with police personnel deployed for maintaining law and order," PTI reported.

Banerjee is the leader of the Trinamool Congress Party, a major regional party in the eastern state of West Bengal. She is the former chief minister of the state and was unseated earlier this year by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party —  after 15 years in power.

Incidentally, at the rally, Banerjee had claimed that the police had turned into a "monstrous entity" under BJP rule and pledged to stop "police atrocities" on her supporters.

Skip next section WATCH — Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the EU dispute

WATCH — Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the EU dispute

The fight over basmati rice has become one of the most complex disputes in the global food trade.

Both India and Pakistan claim the premium, aromatic rice as part of their agriculture and cultural heritage, and both are seeking European Union recognition for its geographical origin.

But years after the first application was filed in 2018, the EU has yet to decide how the name should be protected and by whom.

Basmati is among the world's most valuable rice varieties, generating significant export revenues and carrying strong historical ties to the Punjab region, which spans both countries.

Meanwhile, experts warn that widespread misuse of the name on international markets could undermine future protection altogether. As Brussels weighs its options, the outcome could have far-reaching consequences.

Skip next section Congress slams Penguin India for backing out of Sonia Gandhi's memoir

Congress slams Penguin India for backing out of Sonia Gandhi's memoir

Leaders of India's largest opposition party, the Indian National Congress (INC), alleged that publishing house Penguin India was pressured to back out of publishing veteran politician Sonia Gandhi's memoir due to portions related to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist group, and China's alleged occupation of Indian territory under Modi's rule.

Sonia Gandhi has been a leading figure in Indian politics for decades. She was the president of the INC from 1998 to 2017 and is the party's longest-serving chief.

Earlier this month, Alfred A. Knopf announced that Gandhi's "Belonging: A Journey of Love" will be published on November 10. Knopf is a publishing imprint under Penguin Random House.

"Suppressing the book of Sonia Gandhi, a person of such stature, a senior leader of the nation, and former Leader of the Opposition, under pressure is tantamount to the murder of freedom of Expression," senior INC leader Ashok gehlot said in a post on X.

"The real issue is that pressure was put on Penguin India to remove the portions related to Modi, the RSS, and the occupation of Indian territory by China during Modi's rule. This is the murder of democracy," he said.

In another post, Gehlot said "there's some kind of pressure. It could be from the PMO [Prime Minister's Office] or someone else — that time will tell."

This comes a day after Penguin India released a statement of clarification: "Any suggestion that Penguin Random House India decided not to publish 'Belonging' because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances."

The statement was referring to a report by The Indian Express which said the publishing house would not publish the book in India because "editorial changes and deletions" were turned down by the author.

"As a publisher, it is both our prerogative and our responsibility to fact check and provide authors with recommendations that are in best interests of their books," Penguin India said in its statement, adding that it "remained willing and keen to publish the book."

Skip next section India monitors glaciers after Nepal disaster

India monitors glaciers after Nepal disaster

Days after deadly flash floods triggered by a glacial collapse swept through the Tibet-Nepal border, India stepped up monitoring of the glaciers in its Himalayan region bordering Nepal and China.

Although the exact cause of the collapse remains unclear, global warming has increased the likelihood of such disasters.

"Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbor, and also have a similar geographic situation... we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region," said Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India's Himalayan state of Uttarakhand.

"We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state," he added.

Kaushik's state is one of India's most ecologically sensitive regions with over 1,266 glacial lakes. 

Skip next section Indian Hindu nationalist group's chief set to address thousands in NYC

Indian Hindu nationalist group's chief set to address thousands in NYC

Mohan Bhagwat, the chief of a controversial right-wing Hindu nationalist group in India closely associated with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, is set to address about 5,000 members of Indian American groups in New York City on Saturday. 

The event titled "Universal Oneness Celebration" is being held at the Infosys Theater in Madison Square Garden and is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue.

It is being met with protests, a denunciation from the city's mayor Zohran Mamdani and a call for sanctions by a US panel on religious freedom. 

Bhagwat's link with Modi

Bhagwat is the chief of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for "National Volunteer Organization."

The group describes itself as a "Hindu-centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus. It disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance.

The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization.

Why is the RSS controversial?

In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities.

However, several interfaith and civil rights groups — including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York — have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history.

The US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), a government advisory body, has called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims."

Recently, it called for the US government to impose targeted sanctions on RSS members, including Bhagwat, and Indian officials who support the group.

The Ministry of External Affairs in India quickly rejected the commission’s remarks, calling the body biased and lacking in credibility.

United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more.

Skip next section WATCH: Nepal village buried in mud

WATCH: Nepal village buried in mud

DW correspondent Adil Bhat reports from a village in Nepal's Nuwakot district that was buried in mud after severe flooding.

Skip next section Over 300 Indians still missing in Nepal-Tibet floods

Over 300 Indians still missing in Nepal-Tibet floods

At least 320 Indian nationals were still unaccounted for in the Nepal-Tibet floods as of Friday evening, according to the latest update from India's foreign ministry.

A glacier collapse on Wednesday ‌unleashed a huge torrentof rock, ice, mud and ‌debris ​through Himalayan mountain river systems, killing more than 600 people in Nepal and China's Tibet. Over 2,000 people are missing.

Here's the latest update on Indian nationals:

  • 84 Indian nationals have been rescued so far, including 21 from Tamil Nadu who have returned to India and 63 who were working at the Trishuli-I power project in Nepal
  • 149 crossed over into Nepal from China
  • Around 400 are safe in China, the Indian Embassy in Beijing is working on their evacuation
  • 320 are missing or unreachable

Meanwhile, India dispatched a third flight carrying relief supplies to Nepal on Friday evening. The flight also carried an 11-member medical and tunnel rescue team, who are now working on the ground, according to India's Foreign Minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar.

Skip next section Modi is en route to Uzbekistan for bilateral talks

Modi is en route to Uzbekistan for bilateral talks

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi left for a state visit to Uzbekistan, where he is set to discuss ways of deepening cooperation with President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. 

Ahead of departure, Modi said he looked forward to his discussions with the Uzbek president to "further deepening our cooperation in trade and investment, digital connectivity, defence, energy, and on advancing our shared visions of Viksit Bharat and Yangi Uzbekistan."

"Viksit Bharat" roughly translates to "Developed India" and is a commonly used term by Modi and his ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. "Yangi Uzbekistan" translates to "New Uzbekistan" and is a political slogan used by Mirziyoyev.

On Saturday, Modi will attend a dinner hosted by Mirziyoyev, followed by bilateral engagements with him on Sunday at the Presidential Palace.

After his two-day state visit to Uzbekistan, Modi will travel to the Kyrgyz Republic to attend the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit, where he is also scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting with the Russian President, Vladimir Putin.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello and welcome to DW's India blog!

This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from the Delhi studio and I will be your guide through the chaotic news cycle of the world's most populous nation.

Hundreds of Indians remain missing in the devastating Nepal-Tibet flash floods, as of the Indian foreign ministry's last update. Most of those unaccounted for or stranded were either working in Nepal or were pilgrims visiting the Kailash Mansarovar site in China's Tibet.

Indian embassies in Kathmandu and Beijing are working closely with local authorities, and Delhi has sent at least three tranches of aid.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi embarked on a four-day official trip to Central Asia. He will first visit Uzbekistan to hold bilateral discussions and further cooperation between the two nations. Modi will then attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Kyrgyzstan for the last two days of his tour. 

Stay tuned for all of this and more!

entries.title: Russian strike on ammunition depot near Kyiv kills dozens
entries.summary: Hundreds were also forced to flee after a Russian attack near Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, sparked a huge fire and explosions. The strike was the second to hit an arms depot near Kyiv in less than two months.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Russian strike on ammunition depot near Kyiv kills dozens

August 29, 2026

Hundreds were also forced to flee after a Russian attack near Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, sparked a huge fire and explosions. The strike was the second to hit an arms depot near Kyiv in less than two months.

At least 37 people were killed after a Russian drone strike on a ammunition depot near Kyiv late Friday, one of the deadliest attacks in Ukraine this year.

The drone strike was the second attack to hit an arms depot near the Ukrainian capital in less than two months.

"A terrible situation and terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a video address on X.

"Another such crime — after what happened in Vyshneve — is absolutely unacceptable," he added. Zelenskyy was referring to an attack on an ammunition warehouse last month that set off secondary explosions in the small town on Kyiv's western outskirts, killing ten people.

Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified long-range strikes, increasingly hitting civilian infrastructure such as logistics warehouses and oil and port facilities. These attacks have resulted in more civilian casualties. 

What else do we know about the Russian drone attack near Kyiv?

The strike sparked a major fire and explosions at the arms depot in the Bucha district, close to the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, forcing more than 370 people to evacuate the region. Dozens were injured.

Among those killed was Taras Didych, head of the Dmytrivka community, who was one of the first to rush to the scene to rescue people, according to Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko. He also said the attack damaged at least 50 residential buildings.

Zelenskyy earlier said that criminal proceedings had been opened on charges of official negligence.

"There are regulations in place — ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas," Zelenskyy said.

Kyiv under jet-powered drone attacks

Friday's drone attack followed ​two days of constant air raids aimed at the Ukrainian capital and the surrounding region.

"Kyiv is under virtually nonstop attack from jet-powered drones. Ukraine cannot be left alone in finding solutions to defend against such strikes," said Zelenskyy, adding that Russia also struck nine other regions overnight.

It's been more than four and a half years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbor.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Death toll from Nepal-Tibet floods rises to over 600
entries.summary: Heavy rain is complicating an already difficult rescue effort, as hundreds remain missing three days after deadly flash floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border region.
entries.content:
Nepal

Death toll from Nepal-Tibet floods rises to over 600

August 29, 2026

Heavy rain is complicating an already difficult rescue effort, as hundreds remain missing three days after deadly flash floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border region.

The latest death toll from the devastating flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border was reported on Saturday to be over 600, as frantic rescue operations to search for hundreds of missing people entered a fourth day.

Figures from both countries put the number of missing close to 3,000, with 682 bodies recovered and reports of corpses swept as far downstream as India.

According to Nepal's disaster agency, the death toll there now stands at 675, with 2,426 people — including foreigners — still missing.

Across the border in Tibet, China's state news agency, Xinhua, has confirmed seven deaths and reported 554 missing individuals.

A glacial collapse on Wednesday sent rock, ice, mud and debris surging through the Himalayan mountain river systems below.

The flood swept through areas near the Chinese border, ravaging entire towns and damaging hydropower plants.

What is the status of rescue efforts in Nepal?

Rainy weather conditions are hindering aerial rescue operations in Nepal.

Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told the media on Saturday that helicopter operations were on hold until the weather improved.

Rescuers are battling thick layers of mud in the affected areas, which is making it difficult for helicopters to land and take off.

Tunnels in the mountainous region are also a challenge, Basnet said.

The army has located people trapped in a tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project in Nepal's Rasuwa District. Over 100 people are believed to be inside the tunnel filled with mud.

Basnet said that rescuers were struggling to locate the entry points of the tunnel and had made use of baskets and ropes to reach some people. There are also limited places for helicopters to land in the area.

On Friday, Nepal's Army shared visuals of some people being rescued from the tunnel. The survivors were seen stuck in the mud, while officials crawled through the sludge and held out their hands to them.

On Saturday, Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal said a specialized tunnel rescue team had arrived from neighboring India and was ready to start work.

Nepalese authorities said the bodies of many flood victims have also been found dozens of kilometers from the disaster zone in Chitwan District in southern Nepal, which borders India.

Meanwhile, Indian authorities said they recovered the bodies of seven people who were swept downstream from Nepal and believe them to be flood victims.

Nepal needs help in technical areas, says foreign minister

Late on Friday, Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told the Reuters news agency that his country needed equipment, along with technical knowledge in tunnel rescue operations.

Khanal also told Reuters that Nepal did not need help with search and rescue operations but needed assistance in opening transport and communication lines in places where bridges were destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storage of bodies for a longer timeframe.

"We have already made requests for such ⁠specialized ​services and technical assistance in areas where we don't have enough expertise and technical know-how," ​Reuters quoted Khanal as saying.

Nepal's Foreign Ministry had on Friday declined foreign involvement in search and rescue.

Nepal's post-flood rebuilding estimated at $4-$5 billion

In another Reuters interview, Nepal's Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said that the Himalayan nation may need $4 billion (€3.5 billion) ⁠to $5 billion ⁠to rebuild after the flood.

The estimate is equivalent ​to nearly a tenth of Nepal's economy.

"The initial estimate is ​between $4-$5 billion. Just an estimate," Wagle told Reuters, adding that the bill would be much less than what was needed in reconstruction after the disastrous 2015 earthquake — Nepal's worst ‌ recorded disaster.

"Loss and damage is being assessed," he said.

What do we know about rescue operations in Tibet?

In Gyirong, one of the hardest-hit areas in Tibet along the China-Nepal border, Beijing had temporarily halted its rescue efforts due to the risk of renewed flooding before announcing that the threat had waned.

China's Xinhua agency reported on Saturday morning that two villagers had been rescued in the Gyirong area.

The glacial collapse on Wednesday led to the formation of a barrier lake upstream due to debris dams. Experts warned that the lake had started to overflow.

On Saturday, Chinese authorities announced that the lake had begun to shrink.

China's state broadcaster, CCTV, cited the Ministry of Water Resources as saying that satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake in the Tsangpo River basin on Saturday morning showed a reduction of around 21,000 square meters compared to images from Thursday.

Authorities have also identified a larger body of water at the bottom of the glacier collapse.

"We estimate its area to be over 120,000 ⁠square ​meters, but its depth is currently unknown," Reuters quoted Chen Hongqi, a senior engineer at ​the Ministry of Natural Resources' Geological Disaster Technical Guidance Center, as saying.

Reuters also reported an official of Nepal's Disaster ​Management Authority as saying that flood risks will remain until the two lakes have fully drained.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Niger's defense ministry says soldiers attempted mutiny
entries.summary: Gunfire and explosions were heard across Niamey overnight. The attack posed the latest threat to Niger's military junta, led by Abdourahamane Tchiani, who seized power in a 2023 coup.
entries.content:
Niger

Niger's defense ministry says soldiers attempted mutiny

August 29, 2026

Gunfire and explosions were heard across Niamey overnight. The attack posed the latest threat to Niger's military junta, led by Abdourahamane Tchiani, who seized power in a 2023 coup.

Niger's Ministry of National Defense ‌on ⁠Saturday said ⁠that ​a group of soldiers shot at "sensitive" locations in the capital Niamey in an apparent mutiny.

Gunfire and explosions had been heard across Niger's capital, Niamey, overnight into the early hours of Saturday morning.

Attackers had targeted Diori Hamani International Airport, which also houses a military air base, and attempted to breach the security perimeter around ​the presidency.

"Another cowardly attack on Base 101 and once again our defense and security forces ensured ... Situation under control," said lawmaker Bana Wagana Ibrahim, who serves on the Consultative Council.

Niger military 'gradually regaining control'

The military said it was "gradually regaining control" after mutineers took soldiers hostage at a base near the airport in Niamey, AFP news agency reported.

Authorities urged the public to "remain calm and freely go about their business" in a statement read out on public television and signed by Defense Minister General Salifou Mody.

The attack posed the latest threat to Niger's military junta, led by Abdourahamane Tchiani, who seized power in a 2023 coup.

Niger, like its Sahelian neighbors Mali and Burkina Faso, has for years been ruled by a military junta that has struggled to stem a jihadi insurgency.

National TV signal reportedly cut after gunfire

The shooting began around 1 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) and continued until daybreak.

Locals said that the country's national television had gone off air.

Tele Sahel's satellite and online programming was replaced with a black screen at 9 a.m. local time (0800 GMT), AFP reported. It was restored around one hour later.

Niamey has been targeted by jihadists twice this year: once by the so-called "Islamic State in the Sahel" group (EIS) and again in June by their rivals from the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM).

Edited by: Sean Sinico, Dmytro Hubenko and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Germany news: Sick leave wage bill doubles in 15 years
entries.summary: German firms paid out a record €86 billion in wages to employees on sick leave last year, according to new research. Meanwhile, dozens of firefighters tackled a blaze at a refugee home in Berlin overnight. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Sick leave wage bill doubles in 15 years

Published August 29, 2026last updated August 29, 2026

German firms paid out a record €86 billion in wages to employees on sick leave last year, according to new research. Meanwhile, dozens of firefighters tackled a blaze at a refugee home in Berlin overnight. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • German firms faced a record sick-leave wage bill last year of €86 billion
  • Lower Saxony's state premier calls for deal on Volkswagen restructuring
  • Hundreds of people were evacuated from a fire at a Berlin refugee shelter
  • A Taliban team is in Germany to facilitate Afghan deportations, according to a media report
  • AfD youth wing rejects party plans to leave the euro currency

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, August 29, and Sunday, August 30.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section German government expected to hold Moscow responsible for Leipzig drone incident, reports say

German government expected to hold Moscow responsible for Leipzig drone incident, reports say

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to officially hold Moscow responsible for the Leipzig drone incident in early August, several German news outlets owned by media company Axel Springer SE reported on Saturday.

Berlin is expected to announce the planned move in the coming days, including "extensive" sanctions, three officials familiar with the matter told German newspaper Welt am Sonntag and the media outlet Politico.

However, the three sources did not elaborate on what the specific measures could be. It is also unclear to what extent Berlin plans to hold Russia responsible for the Leipzig incident.

On August 4, a drone loaded with explosives was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport, which serves as a hub for military aid shipments to Ukraine for its war against Russia. 

Merz told RTL in an interview on Thursday that the federal government would soon identify those responsible for the incident.

Skip next section Sick leave now costs Germany twice as much as in 2010

Sick leave now costs Germany twice as much as in 2010

The total amount of wages German firms paid in sick and maternity leave has more than doubled over the past 15 years, a study from the Cologne-based German Economic Institute (IW) shows.

IW estimated that German companies paid a record-high €85.6 billion ($111 billion) in wages to employees who were out sick last year. This compares to €36.9 billion in 2010.

Of the larger figure, €72.5 billion represented gross wages, while €13.1 billion was earmarked for social security contributions.

IW said several factors have contributed to the rise, including wage hikes and inflation in other employee costs.

The institute said the total number of employed people has also grown since 2010, meaning more workers are eligible for sick leave.

IW, however, said it had noted a "significant" rise in recorded sick leave since Germany moved to electronic medical certificates in 2022.

Separate research by the Berlin-based IGES Institute in January showed that German workers now take an average of 19.5 working days as sick leave per year, a noticeable increase from about 13 days in 2018.

In an effort to stem the rise, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government will from January ban patients from receiving sick notes from doctors by phone. 

In Germany, employers are generally required to pay workers' salaries for up to six weeks before the statutory health insurance fund takes over by paying sickness benefits.

Skip next section Lower Saxony premier seeks deal on VW restructuring

Lower Saxony premier seeks deal on VW restructuring

Volkswagen's second-biggest shareholder has called on all sides to agree on a restructuring plan for the German auto giant in the next few days.

Olaf Lies, state premier of Lower Saxony — which holds 18% of VW's shareholder voting rights — said he was convinced "a viable solution" can be found.

"I strongly urge that we ​use the time remaining until the next meeting to bring the different positions together," Lies told journalists on Friday.

The state leader noted that VW must face its numerous business challenges head-on, namely costly tariffs, falling demand and intense competition from China.

But he said the group's position in Germany's industrial landscape ‌also had to be considered.

"With its sites in Lower Saxony and ‌across ​Germany, its tens of thousands of employees and their families, and its suppliers and service providers, Volkswagen also bears an enormous responsibility for the wider economy and society," Lies said.

VW's management now thinks they may need to cut up to 100,000 jobs and that several German factories may face closure.

The supervisory board of Europe's largest automaker is due to meet on September 4 ‌to discuss a ⁠turnaround ⁠plan.

Skip next section Survey: Trump's return increased US influence over Germany

Survey: Trump's return increased US influence over Germany

Two-thirds of residents think the United States has more influence on Germany since US President Donald Trump returned to the White House.

A poll by the Forsa research institute found that 67% of respondents agreed, while just 11% thought there was less US influence. Around 18% thought it was the same.

The survey for the German-language Internationale Politik (International Politics) magazine found only 2% of 18 to 29-year-olds and 6% of 30 to 44-year-olds think US influence in Germany is lower than before Trump's second term. That's versus 18% of respondents aged 60 and over.

Germany-US ties have soured since Trump's reelection, due to surprise tariffs, talk of seizing Greenland and open sniping over Russia's war in Ukraine and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war.

Skip next section Report: Taliban team in Berlin to aid Afghan deportations

Report: Taliban team in Berlin to aid Afghan deportations

The Taliban has sent a team of three people to Germany to help facilitate the deportation of Afghan nationals, public broadcaster NDR reported.

NDR said the delegation arrived in Germany on Wednesday and is staying at the Afghan embassy in Berlin.

The broadcaster said their mission is to provide documents recognized by the Taliban in Kabul to Afghan nationals being deported from Germany.

The delegation is also due to spend time in Bonn and Munich, where Afghanistan has consulates general.

The arrival of the delegation is contentious as Germany — along with most of the rest of the world — does not recognize the Taliban government.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz calls the contacts a purely technical necessity to return people with no right to stay.

Critics, however, say his government is legitimizing the Taliban to help raise deportation numbers.

Germany suspended deportations to Afghanistan when the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

They resumed three years later, initially for convicted criminals.

According to German government data, 15,343 Afghan nationals in Germany are required to leave the country, as of the end of June, including more than 1,500 children.

Skip next section AfD youth wing: Germany shouldn't leave euro

AfD youth wing: Germany shouldn't leave euro

The youth wing of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has broken ranks with party leadership and called for Germany not to leave the euro currency.

"We do not want Germany to leave the euro, but to address the existing structural flaws in the euro system," Jean-Pascal Hohm, head of the Generation Deutschland (GD) youth organization, told the Bild newspaper.

The GD is due to adopt a position on the issue at a conference in the city of Magdeburg on Saturday.

A draft statement says the euro has strengthened the European single market but has "structural flaws," and calls for reforms that would improve stability without giving up Europe's economic unity.

In its 2025 election manifesto, the euroskeptic AfD has called for Germany to leave the euro, the single currency of 21 EU member states.

The GD was established last year as the AfD's new youth organization after the party dissolved its previous youth wing, the Junge Alternative (JA), after it was labeled right-wing extremist by intelligence officials.

Skip next section Hundreds evacuated affter blaze at Berlin refugee shelter

Hundreds evacuated affter blaze at Berlin refugee shelter

A fire broke out early Saturday morning at a refugee shelter in Berlin-Spandau, a borough on the outer western edge of Germany's capital.

The dpa news agency reported that the blaze broke out on the fourth floor of a six-story building, designed to accommodate about 1,200 people

Citing the fire department, dpa said furnishings caught fire in the hallway for reasons yet to be determined.

The smoke then spread to the fifth and sixth floors.

Four people were treated for smoke inhalation, the statement said. Three were taken to hospital.

Several hundred residents were evacuated from the shelter, with between 50 and 60 people moved to alternative accommodation.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning from Bonn, where the Rhine River water level is creeping back up after hitting a low earlier this month during the drought.

Overnight, a fire at a refugee center in Berlin forced the evacuation of hundreds of residents.

A report by public broadcaster NDR reveals that the Taliban has sent a delegation to Germany to help facilitate the deportation of Afghan nationals, whose asylum claims have been rejected.

Also, while the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) wants to leave the euro currency, the party's youth wing has spoken out against the policy, calling instead for "structural flaws" in the euro system to be fixed. 

Here you'll find our coverage of the latest news, sport and analysis from across Germany this weekend.

entries.title: US, Ecuador forces strike alleged drug smuggling boat
entries.summary: Tackling drug trafficking in Latin America is a key priority for Washington. In March, Ecuador joined a US-led coalition to combat the drug trade in the region.
entries.content:
August 29, 2026

Tackling drug trafficking in Latin America is a key priority for Washington. In March, Ecuador joined a US-led coalition to combat the drug trade in the region.

The US military said on Friday it had destroyed an alleged drug trafficking boat in a coordinated operation with Ecuador.

In a post on X, US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said that its forces intercepted a vessel "operating as a floating refueling station" in the Eastern Pacific.

According to SOUTHCOM, the vessel was operating "in support of the Los Choneros violent narco-terrorist organization," referring to one of Ecuador's most powerful criminal gangs, which Washington has designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organization.

"Working together with our Ecuadorian partners, our coalition dealt a decisive blow to a narco-terrorist operation responsible for moving significant amounts of drugs through the region," SOUTHCOM said.

US, Ecuador combat drug cartels

In March, Ecuador joined President Donald Trump's "Shield of the Americas" — a US-led coalition focused on combating drug trafficking across the region.

Ecuador's strategic location between Colombia and Peru — the world's two largest producers of cocaine — makes the country a key transit hub for drug-trafficking gangs.

The US military launched Operation Southern Spear in September 2025 as part of a fight against drug trafficking in the region.

The Trump administration, however, has not presented definitive evidence that the vessels targeted in its operations were carrying or transporting illegal drugs. 

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko
